public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 678
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/678](https://www.erdosproblems.com/678)
- [Ca24] S. Cambie, Resolution of an Erdős' problem on least common multiples. arXiv:2410.09138
  (2024).
- [Er79] Erdős, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
- [Er92e] Erdős, Pál, Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics. Eureka
  (1992), 44-48.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Asymptotics Filter Finset

namespace Erdos678

/--
The referee of [Er79] found the example $M(96, 7) > M(104, 8)$, showing that there are cases where
$M(n, k) > M(m, k + 1)$ with $m \geq n + k$.
[Er79] Erdős, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma lcmInterval_lt_example1 : lcmInterval 104 8 < lcmInterval 96 7 := by decide

/--
The referee of [Er79] found the example $M(132, 7) > M(139, 8)$, showing that there are cases where
$M(n, k) > M(m, k + 1)$ with $m \geq n + k$.
[Er79] Erdős, Paul, Some unconventional problems in number theory. Math. Mag. (1979), 67-70.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma lcmInterval_lt_example2 : lcmInterval 139 8 < lcmInterval 132 7 := by decide

/--
Cambie [Ca24] found the example $M(52, 7) > M(62, 8)$.
[Ca24] S. Cambie, Resolution of an Erdős' problem on least common multiples. arXiv:2410.09138 (2024).
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma lcmInterval_lt_example3 : lcmInterval 62 8 < lcmInterval 52 7 := by decide

/--
Cambie [Ca24] found the example $M(36, 8) > M(48, 9)$.
[Ca24] S. Cambie, Resolution of an Erdős' problem on least common multiples. arXiv:2410.09138 (2024).
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma lcmInterval_lt_example4 : lcmInterval 47 9 < lcmInterval 36 8 := by decide

/--
Write $M(n, k)$ be the least common multiple of $\{n+1, \dotsc, n+k\}$.
Let $k$ be sufficiently large. Are there infinitely many $m, n$ with $m \geq n + k$ such that
$$
M(n, k) > M(m, k + 1)
$$?
The answer is yes, as proved in a strong form by Cambie [Ca24].
[Ca24] S. Cambie, Resolution of an Erdős' problem on least common multiples. arXiv:2410.09138 (2024).

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle, on top of the PNT+ project.

For a fixed $k$ there are only finitely many such pairs, so "infinitely many" is read here as
ranging over $k$ as well: for every sufficiently large $k$ at least one pair $(m, n)$ occurs.
See `erdos_678.variants.infinitely_many_triples` for the reading in which the infinitude is
stated directly, and `erdos_678.variants.not_infinitely_many_pairs` for why it cannot be asked
of a single $k$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/68da20b96673899166e94638f5a7fffeb7231d35/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos678.lean"]
theorem erdos_678 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ᶠ k in atTop, {(m, n) | n + k ≤ m ∧ lcmInterval m (k + 1) < lcmInterval n k}.Nonempty := by
  sorry

/--
The pairs $(m, n)$ with $m \geq n + k$ and $M(n, k) > M(m, k + 1)$ are infinite in number once
$k$ is allowed to vary, which is the sense in which Cambie's result answers the question.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/68da20b96673899166e94638f5a7fffeb7231d35/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos678.lean"]
theorem erdos_678.variants.infinitely_many_triples :
    {(k, m, n) | 3 ≤ k ∧ n + k ≤ m ∧ lcmInterval m (k + 1) < lcmInterval n k}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
For a fixed sufficiently large $k$ only finitely many pairs occur: $M(m, k + 1) \geq m + 1$
bounds $m$ by $M(n, k)$, and for large $n$ the inequality reverses. So the question cannot be
read as asking for infinitely many pairs at a single $k$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/68da20b96673899166e94638f5a7fffeb7231d35/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos678.lean"]
theorem erdos_678.variants.not_infinitely_many_pairs :
    ¬ ∀ᶠ k in atTop, {(m, n) | n + k ≤ m ∧ lcmInterval m (k + 1) < lcmInterval n k}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos678

findings.description: The source asks whether there are infinitely many triples (m, n, k) with k ≥ 3, m ≥ n+k and M(n,k) > M(m,k+1). Write S_k = {(m,n) | n+k ≤ m ∧ lcmInterval m (k+1) < lcmInterval n k}. Every S_k is finite: M(m,k+1) ≥ m+1 bounds m, and for large n the inequality reverses. So the question is equivalent to `∃ᶠ k in atTop, S_k.Nonempty`, i.e. to `erdos_678.variants.infinitely_many_triples`. `erdos_678` instead states `answer(True) ↔ ∀ᶠ k in atTop, S_k.Nonempty`. That is Cambie's Theorem 1 with C = 1, which Cambie calls 'the following stronger result' and the source records only as the answer 'in a strong form'. I proved in a scratch file that the ∀ᶠ form implies the triples form. The converse is not a logical consequence: if pairs existed only for even k, the source's question would hold and the Lean would fail. Both statements are true (Cambie), so `answer(True)` asserts nothing false. Still, the main declaration poses a strictly stronger claim than the one asked; the posed question appears only as a variant. The docstring's justification does not work: letting 'infinitely many' range over k gives infinitely many k, not every sufficiently large k. The docstring also quotes the problem as 'Let k be sufficiently large. Are there infinitely many m, n with m ≥ n + k ...'. That wording is neither the source's current statement nor the previous one in the site's revision history ('Let k≥3. Are there infinitely many m,n with m≥n+k ...').
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/678 (LaTeX page https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/678; Wayback snapshots 2026-01-29 and 2026-08-24; 'last edited 11 January 2026'): 'Are there infinitely many $m,n$ and $k\geq 3$ with $m\geq n+k$ such that $M(n,k)>M(m,k+1)$? ... The description in [Er79] is ambiguous whether the problem intended is the above, or to take a fixed $k\geq 3$ ... Presumably Erdős intended to ask the problem above ... The answer is yes, as proved in a strong form by Cambie [Ca24], who proved that for all sufficiently large $k$ there exist $m\geq n+k$ with this property.' Cambie, arXiv:2410.09138, Sec. 1: 'Erdős posed the question whether there exist infinitely many cases in which the lcm of the larger such set is smaller than the lcm of the smaller set. ... We answer the question by giving an elementary proof for the following stronger result' (Theorem 1: for every k sufficiently large there exist 0<x<y with y>x+k and lcm{x,...,x+k-1} > C·lcm{y,...,y+k}).
findings.suggested_fix: Make the posed question the main theorem: `theorem erdos_678 : answer(True) ↔ {(k, m, n) | 3 ≤ k ∧ n + k ≤ m ∧ lcmInterval m (k + 1) < lcmInterval n k}.Infinite` (the current `infinitely_many_triples`). Move the current `∀ᶠ k in atTop, {...}.Nonempty` statement to a variant such as `erdos_678.variants.cambie`, with a docstring citing Cambie's Theorem 1. Quote the source's current wording in the main docstring.

findings.description: The docstring says 'Cambie [Ca24] found the example $M(36, 8) > M(48, 9)$'. The Lean states `lcmInterval 47 9 < lcmInterval 36 8`, i.e. M(36,8) > M(47,9). The Lean matches Cambie's example; the docstring is off by one and its inequality is false. M(48,9) = lcm{49,...,57} = 647,745,298,200 is larger than M(36,8) = 148,875,406,680, while M(47,9) = 68,183,715,600. Checked by `decide`: `¬ (lcmInterval 48 9 < lcmInterval 36 8)` and `lcmInterval 47 9 = (Finset.Icc 48 56).lcm id`.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to 'Cambie [Ca24] found the example $M(36, 8) > M(47, 9)$.' The Lean statement is correct as is.

review.notes:
No declaration in the file asserts anything false, and nothing is vacuous or trivially provable. The two findings are (1) the main theorem states Cambie's strong form instead of the posed question, which sits in the variant `infinitely_many_triples`, and (2) an off-by-one in a test-lemma docstring.

Checks done:
- Lean scratch files: (a) the main theorem's `∀ᶠ k, S_k.Nonempty` implies `{(k,m,n) | 3 ≤ k ∧ ...}.Infinite` (proved); (b) in general ∃ᶠ does not imply ∀ᶠ (proved abstractly with P = Even); (c) `decide` checks for example 4.
- A bounded search finds pairs for k = 7..13 and none for k ≤ 6 in the window. The first pairs for k = 7 and k = 8 match Cambie's minimal examples.
- The other test lemmas (Selfridge's M(96,7) > M(104,8) and M(132,7) > M(139,8); Cambie's M(52,7) > M(62,8)) match their sources and satisfy m ≥ n+k.

`erdos_678.variants.infinitely_many_triples` is exactly the source's current question. `ℕ` in place of positive integers is immaterial: n = 0 can give solutions for at most finitely many k, since lcm(1..k) < C(2k+1,k+1) ≤ M(m,k+1) for large k.

`erdos_678.variants.not_infinitely_many_pairs` states `¬ ∀ᶠ k, S_k.Infinite`. That is the negation of the 'fixed large k, infinitely many pairs' reading, which the source says is easily disproved. It is weaker than its docstring's first sentence ('for a fixed sufficiently large k only finitely many pairs occur'); in fact every S_k is finite, so it could be strengthened to `∀ k, S_k.Finite`. Its conclusion is faithful, so I did not file a finding.

Status: all three theorems are tagged research solved with formal_proof links. That is consistent with erdosproblems.com ('PROVED (LEAN)') and the teorth database ('proved (Lean)', 2026-01-07). The linked plby file contains `erdos_678`: Cambie's Theorem 1 with C = 1, in x = n+1, y = m+1 notation with y > x+k, which implies the FC main statement. It also contains `erdos_678_kmn_infinite`, identical to `infinitely_many_triples`, and `not_erdos_678_fc`, identical to `not_infinitely_many_pairs`.

Limitations:
- I could not read [Er79] (the Rényi PDF is a scanned image and no OCR tool is available) or [Er92e] (not in the online archive). I relied on erdosproblems.com's summary of them and on Cambie's account.
- Archive.org blocked the 2024 and early-2025 snapshots, so I could not tell whether the docstring's 'Let k be sufficiently large' wording ever appeared on the site. The site's revision history shows only the earlier 'Let k≥3' wording.
- I deliberately did not read the erdosproblems.com forum thread, since it may discuss this repository's formalization.
